analysis.step_by_step_reasoning: 1) The whiteboard shows a generic 'AWS' cloud icon feeding Apache Metron. The speaker explicitly lists the AWS telemetry sources behind it (S3, SNS, SQS, CloudTrail, GuardDuty), so per the audio-driven expansion rule the generic node is expanded into five source nodes, each sending to Apache Metron. Apache NiFi (AWS side) and syslog/Kafka (on-prem side) are mentioned only as integration mechanisms and are not drawn, so they are recorded in notes rather than added as nodes. 2) On-Prem is drawn with an arrow into Apache Metron. 3) Apache Metron is drawn with an EC2 icon but is a named external product, so it is ThirdParty. It parses, enriches and profiles events. 4) Security Data Lake box: Metron -> EMR -> S3 -> Athena, as drawn and as described (an EMR job moves persisted HDFS data to S3; Athena queries S3). The data lake S3 is kept separate from the S3 telemetry source because they play different roles. 5) The long pink curve from the right edge of the Security Data Lake box back up to Apache Metron is the feedback loop described in the audio (long-term profiles/models fed back to Metron). Its exact origin inside the box is ambiguous; I attributed it to Athena, the analytics end of the lake, as a meta edge. 6) Response flow: Metron -> SOAR (the 'Blitz' orchestration framework, drawn as EC2) -> Alerts (SOC analyst) -> WAF. The analyst is kept because it is drawn as an explicit step on the path and actively triggers the block action; removing it would create a shortcut. 7) Flows: 0 = hybrid ingestion, 1 = data lake persistence, analytics and feedback, 2 = incident response.

graph.name: MakeMyTrip: Next-Gen SOC with Apache Metron and a Serverless Security Data Lake
graph.notes: Next-gen SOC built from the ground up by MakeMyTrip. Hybrid telemetry (AWS and on-premises) is ingested into Apache Metron for parsing, enrichment and profiling. A security data lake (EMR, S3, Athena) stores telemetry for months or years and feeds long-term profiles back to Metron. A SOAR platform (Blitz, open source) enriches alerts and presents them to SOC analysts, who can respond with one click, e.g. blocking a source on the WAF. Scale: about 20 data sources, about 5000 events per second, about 250 million events indexed per day in the data lake. Example use case: detecting server compromise through deviation of the producer/consumer ratio (PCR). The generic 'AWS' icon on the whiteboard was expanded into the services named in the audio.

nodes.name: S3 (telemetry source)
nodes.notes: AWS public cloud telemetry source named in the audio; part of the generic 'AWS' icon on the whiteboard. Events are pulled into Apache Metron through Apache NiFi workflows.

nodes.notes: AWS public cloud telemetry source named in the audio; part of the generic 'AWS' icon. Integrated through Apache NiFi.

nodes.name: GuardDuty
nodes.notes: AWS public cloud telemetry source named in the audio; part of the generic 'AWS' icon. GuardDuty log messages are parsed into JSON by Metron.

nodes.name: On-Prem
nodes.notes: On-premises data sources. Standard syslog or Kafka integration pulls events directly into Apache Metron.

nodes.name: Apache Metron
nodes.notes: Heart of the next-gen SOC (drawn with an EC2 icon). Parses telemetry into a JSON format, enriches it with contextual intelligence (geolocation, AS number, server role such as flight/hotel/payment) and builds short-term profiles in the stream processing layer. Originally persisted to HDFS. About 20 data sources, about 5000 events per second.

nodes.name: EMR
nodes.notes: Part of the Security Data Lake. An EMR job picks up persisted data from Metron's HDFS and transforms it into S3.

nodes.name: S3 (Security Data Lake)
nodes.notes: Long-term storage of telemetry for months or years in the Security Data Lake, migrated from on-prem HDFS. About 250 million events indexed per day.

nodes.name: Athena
nodes.notes: SQL queries and analytics over S3 for log mining, analytics, forensics and future threat hunting. Supports long-term profiles and models over months of telemetry.

nodes.name: SOAR
nodes.notes: Security orchestration and response platform called Blitz (open source on GitHub). Takes alerts from Metron, adds further context (reverse DNS, whois lookup) and presents them in a single pane of glass, on mobile or via a Jira integration.

nodes.name: Alerts (SOC analyst)
nodes.notes: SOC analysts receive the enriched alerts, which cuts triage and investigation time, and can respond at the click of a button.

nodes.name: WAF
nodes.notes: Mitigation target for semi-automated response, e.g. blocking a source. Firewalls and internal routers are also mentioned as integrations.

analysis.step_by_step_reasoning: 1) Inventory: the board shows a central AWS account (Security Engineers, QuickSight, Athena, a hand-drawn S3 findings bucket, MySQL, Glue, Macie) and two further AWS accounts, each with Macie and S3. 2) Pruning: Security Engineers is a generic human actor with no arrows, so it is removed. 3) Fusion: the three Macie icons act as one multi-account Macie deployment (production accounts connected to Macie), so they are fused into one node. The two member-account S3 icons are fused into one 'production S3 buckets' node (the scan targets). The central hand-drawn bucket is kept separate because it plays a different role (findings/results bucket). 4) MySQL is not an AWS service icon, so it is typed ThirdParty ('MySQL data lake'). 5) Edges from drawn arrows: Macie -> findings S3, Athena -> findings S3 (query), QuickSight -> findings S3 (the speaker says this is done via Athena), findings S3 -> MySQL. 6) Edges from the audio only: production S3 buckets -> Macie (Macie inventories and scans the buckets), and findings S3 -> Glue (Glue automations get, load and aggregate the data). Glue has no drawn arrow, so the Glue edge is an interpretation of the transcript. 7) Flows: flow 0 = discovery and findings delivery; flow 1 = query and dashboarding; flow 2 = load/aggregation into the MySQL data lake for remediation reporting.

graph.name: Oportun: Sensitive Data Discovery and DSPM with Amazon Macie
graph.notes: Multi-account Amazon Macie scans production S3 buckets for sensitive member data (SSNs, ITINs, government IDs). Findings (metadata only, no PII) land in a company-owned S3 bucket, are queried with Athena, visualized in QuickSight, and loaded into a MySQL data lake with Glue automations to identify bucket owners and remediate. Reported accuracy of automated sensitive data discovery for patterns such as SSNs and ITINs is 95%.

nodes.name: Production S3 Buckets (member AWS accounts)
nodes.notes: S3 buckets in the connected production AWS accounts. Macie inventories them and the team selects which ones to scan. Fused from the two member-account S3 icons.

nodes.name: Amazon Macie
nodes.notes: Data discovery tool connected across multiple AWS accounts, with production accounts prioritized. Quickly inventories all S3 buckets and runs manual or scheduled scans. Automated sensitive data discovery accuracy is 95% for patterns/regexes such as SSNs and ITINs. Fused from the three Macie icons.

nodes.name: Amazon S3 (Macie findings bucket)
nodes.notes: Company-owned bucket set up per connected account to receive Macie results. Holds only metadata (e.g. number of SSNs per bucket); no PII or sensitive data.

nodes.name: Amazon Athena
nodes.notes: SQL-based query tool that looks into the findings buckets and queries the findings information.

nodes.name: Amazon QuickSight
nodes.notes: Dashboards showing the top 10/20/30 risky buckets by PII type and their owners, used to drive remediation. Other BI tools such as Tableau or Power BI could be used instead.

nodes.name: MySQL
nodes.notes: MySQL data lake built by the company, into which findings data is dropped to identify bucket owners and support remediation.

nodes.name: AWS Glue
nodes.notes: Automations that get, load and aggregate the findings data for reporting to data owners. No arrow is drawn to it on the board.
